chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Safwan al-Jammal who said:

I was afflicted with nabidh, being fond of it, so I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, let me describe nabidh to you.' He said, 'I will describe it to you. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and that which its much intoxicates, its little is forbidden."'

I said to him, 'This is the nabidh of the Siqayah (watering of pilgrims) in the courtyard of the Kaaba.' He said, 'It was not thus; rather the Siqayah is Zamzam. Do you know who first changed it?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib. He had a habalah. Do you know what the habalah is?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'The vineyard. So he would soak raisins in the morning and they would drink it in the evening, and soak it in the evening and they would drink it in the morning, intending to break the thickness of the water for the people. And indeed these have transgressed, so do not approach it and do not drink it.'

key_terms.الْحَبَلَةُ: Habalah (a vineyard or place of grapes)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on nabidh and how did Al-Abbas change the Siqayah?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the specific ruling on *nabidh* by distinguishing between the original Zamzam-based *Siqayah* and the later innovation introduced by Al-Abbas, who used raisins (*habalah*) to create a mildly intoxicating drink. He highlights the principle of *kathiruhu wa qaliluhu haram* (abundance and scarcity are alike) by noting that while the drink was initially used to mitigate the harshness of water, the subsequent transgression in its preparation and consumption led to its prohibition, illustrating the Shia scholarly emphasis on preventing the means to intoxication (*sabab al-khamr*).
